hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when did you last say thank you out loud, to someone’s face, not in a text?
options: lovely. you’re already halfway into this story.
that’s okay. this story is about getting back to it.
so do i, mostly. watch what this man does.

steps.line: In Luke’s Gospel, Jesus came to a village. Ten men with leprosy stood far off and called out: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”

steps.q: Why do the ten men stand so far off?
o: The law kept people with skin disease apart
steps.why: Leviticus told people with skin disease to live apart and call out a warning. Only a priest could declare them clean and let them come home.

steps.line: He told them: go, show yourselves to the priests. A priest could declare them clean, and let them come home.

steps.q: They set off for the priests, still sick. What do you think happens on the road?
o: Nothing, until a priest sees them
They lose heart and turn back
steps.why: They’re healed on the way. They trusted his word before anything had changed.

steps.line: And as they went, they were healed.
One of them, seeing he was healed, turned back, praising God at the top of his voice.
He fell at Jesus’s feet and thanked him. He was a Samaritan, from a people many Jews of his day kept apart from.
“Weren’t ten made clean?” said Jesus. “Where are the nine?” Then to the man: “Get up and go. Your faith has made you whole.”

steps.q: Luke’s Greek for “made you whole” is a word he uses elsewhere for something bigger. What?
steps.why: Sesōken: “has saved you.” All ten were made clean; many readers hear that this one received something more.

steps.line: Today: the family dinner where everyone names one thing they’re thankful for. Half the table groans. It still counts. Out loud counts.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Jesus sent all ten to the priests. Where would a Samaritan’s own priests have been?
o: On Mount Gerizim, their holy mountain
steps.why: Samaritans had their own priests and holy mountain, Gerizim, and the two peoples were bitterly split. Some readers notice he turned back to Jesus before going anywhere.

say: here’s what i love. he didn’t wait for the perfect words. he just turned around and said it, loudly, in the dust.
in christian teaching, thanks isn’t a mood you wait for. an old line says it: in every thing give thanks. not only when it’s easy. said out loud, even badly, it still counts.

steps.q: Why might Luke point out that the one who came back was a Samaritan?
o: Samaritans had a law about giving thanks
Thanks came from the least expected one
Luke’s first readers were mostly Samaritans
steps.why: Luke also tells the parable of the Good Samaritan. Again and again in his Gospel, the outsider is the one who gets it right.

today.say: today, say three thank-yous out loud: to a person, or, if you pray, it’s your choice to say them to god. they can be tiny: warm socks, the bus that came. say them badly. thank you anyway.
options: good. turn around, like he did, and say it.
it will, a little. whisper them. that counts too.

sources: Luke 17:11–19 (KJV): going to Jerusalem, through the midst of Samaria and Galilee; ten lepers stand afar off and lift up their voices, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us”; “Go shew yourselves unto the priests”; “as they went, they were cleansed”; one, when he saw that he was healed, turned back and with a loud voice glorified God, fell down on his face at his feet giving him thanks, “and he was a Samaritan”; “Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?”; “Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole.”
Leviticus 13:45–46 and 14:1–32: the person with skin disease dwells apart; the priest examines and declares clean.
1 Thessalonians 5:18, “In every thing give thanks” (KJV), quoted unnamed in the teach.

check: Biblical “leprosy” covers a range of skin diseases; captions keep the familiar word and the why says “skin disease.” Confirm.
“A people many Jews of his day kept apart from” simplifies the tensions between Jews and Samaritans. Confirm the wording.
“Made you whole” (KJV); the Greek sesoken can also mean “saved you.” The fill’s why says the one who came back “heard something more.” Confirm this reading.
Paintings show the ten in hooded cloaks with no visible disease, and Jesus only from behind. Confirm.
